message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
# Memo

**To:** Director of Operations, Brookside Veterinary Group
**From:** [Analyst]
**Date:** 13 November 2026
**Re:** Evening and Saturday hours pilot at 3 clinics in 2027

## Recommendation

**No-go on the pilot as proposed.** Instead, approve a smaller test: Saturday-only hours at one northern-suburbs clinic from April 2027. Expand only if that test meets clear volume targets.

## Why not the full pilot

**1. The volume needed to break even is higher than the evidence supports.**
- Each clinic would add 28 hours a week at about $310 an hour, or $8,680 a week.
- Each urgent visit contributes about $204 ($340 × 60%).
- Each clinic therefore needs about 43 visits a week, or 1.5 per open hour, just to cover staffing.
- Across 3 clinics, that is about 550 visits a month.

The after-hours phone line receives 1,140 calls a month for all 9 clinics. About 730 of those (64%) are treatable urgent cases. However, many of those calls come overnight, on Sundays or on holidays, which the pilot would not cover. Some are repeat calls about the same pet, and not every caller would drive to one of only 3 open clinics. Breaking even would require converting roughly three-quarters of all treatable after-hours calls across the network into pilot visits. That is implausible without substantial new demand, and we have no evidence of that demand. At full scale, the pilot commits about $1.35 million a year in staffing before any vet pay premium.

**2. We cannot staff it reliably.**
- We already have 4 unfilled veterinarian positions.
- 70% of current veterinarians will not work regular evenings.
- Evening recruits expect a 20–25% premium, which raises the break-even volume further.
- The pilot needs about 84 veterinarian-hours a week, roughly two full-time vets. Pulling existing vets onto evening shifts would worsen daytime gaps.

**3. It puts an existing referral stream at risk.**
Valley Animal Emergency sends us about 300 follow-up patients a year, and its owner has signalled she may reconsider this. Losing those referrals would partly offset any gains, and that loss would begin before the pilot proves itself.

## Why not do nothing

The demand signal is real. 72% of clients say they would prefer to come to us for urgent care. A competitor has opened two urgent-care clinics in the past year. If we wait, we risk giving up this market permanently.

## Proposed smaller test

- **Saturday hours, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., at one northern clinic.** Six of our 9 clinics are in the northern suburbs, so most of our clients are there.
- **Cost:** about $2,500 a week, or roughly $130,000 a year. Break-even is about 12 visits per Saturday.
- **Staffing:** covered by the roughly 30% of vets willing to work extra hours, paid at a premium, with no new hires needed.
- **Before the end of the month:**
  - Log after-hours calls by hour and day.
  - Record each caller's nearest clinic.
- **Before launch:** meet Valley's owner to agree on what cases each side handles. One option is to keep referring overnight and true emergency cases to Valley.
- **Expansion trigger:** if Saturday visits average 15 or more over 3 months, extend to evenings at the same clinic, then to a second site.

This approach tests real demand at about a tenth of the cost and protects the Valley relationship. It also gives us a defensible basis for a larger decision in late 2027.

---

##
</document>
response:
# Review: Evening and Saturday Hours Pilot Memo

The memo is clear and decisive, and most of the numbers check out. The no-go case is well supported. The main problems are in the **proposed smaller test**: its cost figure leaves out the vet premium the memo itself cites, its break-even is rounded down, and its expansion trigger sits too close to break-even to show anything.

## Arithmetic check

| Claim | Check | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 28 hrs × $310 = $8,680/week | 8,680 | ✅ |
| $340 × 60% = $204 | 204 | ✅ |
| ~43 visits/week, 1.5/hour | 42.5; 1.52 | ✅ |
| ~550 visits/month across 3 clinics | 127.6 × 4.33 ≈ 553 | ✅ |
| ~¾ of 730 treatable calls | 553 / 730 ≈ 76% | ✅ |
| ~$1.35M/year | 8,680 × 3 × 52 = $1,354,080 | ✅ |
| 84 vet-hours ≈ 2 FTE | 84 / 40 = 2.1 | ✅ |
| Saturday test ≈ $130k/year | 2,500 × 52 = $130,000 | ✅ |
| Break-even ≈ 12 visits/Saturday | 2,500 / 204 = 12.25, so **13** are needed | ⚠️ Rounded down |
| "About a tenth of the cost" | 130k / 1.35M ≈ 9.6% | ✅ |

## Substantive issues

**1. The Saturday test cost leaves out the premium.**
$2,500 for 8 hours is about $312/hour, which is the base rate. But the memo says Saturday vets will be "paid at a premium," and evening recruits expect 20–25% more. With that premium, the cost is closer to **$3,000–3,100 a week**, and break-even rises to **about 15 visits**. The expansion trigger is also 15, so it would only confirm break-even, not success. Recost the test and set the trigger clearly above break-even, for example 18–20 visits.

**2. "75% of calls" understates how hard break-even is.**
The 730 treatable calls cover all hours, including overnight, Sundays and holidays, which the memo itself excludes. The real comparison is pilot-hour calls only, and those could make the required capture rate approach or exceed 100%. Even rough data would strengthen point 1 considerably. Two caveats point the other way and should be acknowledged:
- Walk-ins who never call the line are not counted.
- Some evening visits would be existing daytime patients shifting their time. That is cannibalization, not new revenue, and it supports the no-go.

**3. The staffing logic doesn't carry over to Saturdays.**
"70% won't work regular evenings" does not show that the other 30% will work Saturdays. Also, "no new hires needed" sits uneasily next to 4 unfilled positions, because extra Saturday shifts load people who are already stretched. Ask the vets directly about Saturday availability before launch.

**4. The choice of the northern site rests on clinic count, not client data.**
Having 6 of 9 clinics in the north does not prove most clients are there. Use client addresses or visit volumes. Also say which clinic, and why it beats the others, for example competitor proximity or call origin.

**5. The Valley risk isn't quantified.**
300 referrals a year is meaningful, but the memo gives no dollar value. Even a rough estimate, such as 300 × average follow-up contribution, would show how much weight this risk deserves. Also note that the Saturday test could itself unsettle Valley, which is why the pre-launch meeting matters.

**6. The 72% survey figure needs context.**
Stated preference is not behaviour. Give the sample size and the exact question wording. Also reconcile this figure with point 1: if demand is real, why is the volume implausible? Price, distance and timing are likely reasons, and saying so would strengthen the argument.

**7. Smaller points:**
- Say what $310/hour includes (vet, techs, reception, overheads?) and what the 60% margin covers.
- Explain the April 2027 start. Why wait about 5 months if no hires are needed?
- A 3-month window from April to June may be affected by seasonality. Name this risk.
- Add success metrics beyond visit count: new client acquisition, Valley referral retention and staff burnout or turnover.
- The memo doesn't summarise what the original proposal projected. One line on its assumptions would show where the analysis differs.

## Formatting

- There is an empty `##` heading after the final `---`. Remove it.
- Replace the `[Analyst]` placeholder.
- In "Before the end of the month," say which month. The date is 13 November, so that leaves only about 2.5 weeks of call logging.

## Bottom line

Keep the recommendation; it is well reasoned. Before sending, fix issue 1 (recost with the premium and raise the trigger), and tighten issues 2 and 3. Those are the points a sceptical director is most likely to challenge.
